title: The cell of self-knowledge
hookLine: Catherine asks us to live in a cell of knowing ourselves and God's goodness
tomorrow: is crying ever a kind of prayer?

cards: Noise-canceling headphones: one click, and the bus, the café and the group project all go quiet. A room you carry in your ears. Catherine of Siena had something like it, without the battery.

The story told about her youth is that her family, pressing her toward marriage, took away the small room where she prayed and filled her days with housework. So she built a room inside herself, one nobody could take.

teach.b: In the Dialogue that inner room becomes the cell of self-knowledge. The book opens with a soul staying in that cell, the better to know God's goodness toward her. Second, what the cell is for.
It isn't a room of mirrors, where you stare at yourself until you sink or swell. It has a window. Catherine pairs the two kinds of knowing, each one seasoning the other.

In the Dialogue the Father warns against each half alone. Knowing your faults without knowing his goodness can drag a soul down into confusion. Knowing his goodness without knowing yourself can puff a soul up.
Held together, they make humility, which here means simply the truth: small, and loved. Fourth, the sound of it. A cell, in a convent or a monastery, is a plain, quiet room.
Catherine's is quiet too, but portable.
You can be in it at a sink full of dishes, which is where the story says she learned it.

how: Catholics practice self-knowledge in the daily examen and before confession, looking honestly at the day while giving thanks for God's gifts; Catherine's inner cell is a classic picture of it.

games.q: what does “the cell of self-knowledge” mean?
o: a course of study for new nuns in Catherine's day
a convent room kept locked for a nun's confession
Catherine's inner room of honesty about self and God

games.q: the cell of self-knowledge — tap the pairs.
p: can drag a soul into confusion

s: self-knowledge for Catherine means dwelling on your faults
she pairs it with knowing God's goodness; faults alone can drag a soul down.
the story says she built an inner cell after her own room was taken
her family filled her days with housework; she made a room inside.
the cell is a place to shut God out and think things through alone
the soul stays there the better to know God's goodness toward her.

games.q: after a breakup your friend says, "i'm going to focus on me for a while, figure out who i am." what would Catherine's cell add?
o: look honestly at yourself, and at the good you've been given; both together.
nothing; self-knowledge means looking only at yourself, nothing else.
skip it; looking inward always makes heartbreak worse.
games.why: in Catherine's cell, knowing yourself goes with knowing God's goodness. either half alone sinks you or swells you.

practice: Listen to the room you're in, one sound at a time: a hum, a car outside, your own breath. Let this ordinary room be the cell.
Inside it, name one true thing about yourself and one good thing you've been given, and keep the two side by side until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: The cell of self-knowledge. Catherine's inner room, where you see yourself honestly and God's goodness clearly, both at once.

orig.note: Latin: a small room or storeroom, the word for a monk's or nun's room, and Catherine's image for the inner room.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the inner cell, a room nobody can take, with a window on God's goodness. Until tomorrow.
